question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Mr. Rao (a)/ has left the office just now, (b)/ so you may meet him (c)/ tomorrow morning. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Just now" means "a moment ago" and points to a definite past time, so it takes the simple past and not the present perfect. (Contrast "just" alone, which goes with the present perfect: "He has just left.") So "has left the office just now" must be "left the office just now".

◦ Corrected sentence: Mr. Rao left the office just now, so you may meet him tomorrow morning.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Mr. Rao" is proper, as a singular subject that agrees with the verb in part (b).

 

• Part (c) is correct — "so you may meet him" is proper, with "so" showing the result and "may" followed by the base verb "meet".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "tomorrow morning." is proper, because "tomorrow morning" takes no preposition.

 

NOTE

 

• He left just now, She arrived just now (simple past with "just now"); but He has just left (present perfect with "just").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

When have you received (a)/ the notice from (b)/ the bank? (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A question that begins with the interrogative "When" asks about a definite past time, so the simple past is used and not the present perfect. So "When have you received" must be "When did you receive".

◦ Corrected sentence: When did you receive the notice from the bank?

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the notice from" is proper, with "the notice" as a specific document and "from" naming its source.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "the bank?" is proper, with "the" used before a specific bank.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "have you received" in part (a) is a present perfect used with "When".

 

NOTE

 

• When did you receive the letter?, When did she leave? (simple past after "when"); but Have you received the letter yet? (present perfect without "when").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The Rajdhani Express (a)/ leaves New Delhi at (b)/ 4.30 tomorrow afternoon. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is grammatically correct. The simple present is used for a future event fixed by a timetable or schedule (trains, flights, classes, shows), so "leaves … tomorrow afternoon" is correct.

◦ Sentence as given: The Rajdhani Express leaves New Delhi at 4.30 tomorrow afternoon.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The Rajdhani Express" is proper, with "The" used before the name of a specific train and a singular subject.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "leaves New Delhi at" is proper, with the singular verb "leaves" and "at" used before a clock time.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "4.30 tomorrow afternoon." is proper, because "tomorrow afternoon" takes no preposition.

 

NOTE

 

• The train leaves at 6 a.m. tomorrow, The exam starts next Monday, The shop closes at nine (simple present for a scheduled future event).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

My uncle (a)/ has gone to Singapore several times (b)/ on business trips, (c)/ and he enjoys them. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Has / have gone to" means the person has gone there and is still away, while "has / have been to" means the person has visited and has come back. A repeated visit ("several times") needs "has been to", so "has gone to" must be "has been to".

◦ Corrected sentence: My uncle has been to Singapore several times on business trips, and he enjoys them.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "My uncle" is proper, as a singular subject that takes "has".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "on business trips," is proper, with "on" used before "business trips".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "and he enjoys them." is proper, with the plural "them" referring to "trips".

 

NOTE

 

• She has been to Paris twice (visited and returned); She has gone to Paris (she is there now).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

He behaves as if he is (a)/ the owner of (b)/ the company, though (c)/ he is only a trainee. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After "as if / as though", the past subjunctive ("were") is used when the comparison is contrary to fact. He is only a trainee, so "as if he is" must be "as if he were".

◦ Corrected sentence: He behaves as if he were the owner of the company, though he is only a trainee.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the owner of" is proper, with "the" before "owner" and "of" showing ownership.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "the company, though" is proper, with "though" introducing the contrast.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "he is only a trainee." is proper, with the simple present "is" for an actual fact and "a" before the consonant sound of "trainee".

 

NOTE

 

• He talks as if he were a king, She behaves as though she knew everything (past tense / "were" for an unreal comparison).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

By next March, (a)/ Dr. Rao (b)/ will be teaching here (c)/ for twenty years. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• An action that continues for a period up to a future time takes the future perfect continuous ("will have been + verb-ing"). "By next March" and "for twenty years" together point to it, so "will be teaching" must be "will have been teaching".

◦ Corrected sentence: By next March, Dr. Rao will have been teaching here for twenty years.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "By next March," is proper, with "By" showing a deadline and "next March" taking no preposition.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "Dr. Rao" is proper, as a singular subject.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "for twenty years." is proper, with "for" used before a period of time.

 

NOTE

 

• By June, she will have been working here for ten years (future perfect continuous); By June, she will have completed the project (future perfect).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

This is the most moving film (a)/ that I saw so far (b)/ in my career as a critic. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After a superlative ("the most moving", "the best", "the worst"), the present perfect (often with "ever" or "so far") is used for an experience up to now. So "that I saw so far" must be "that I have seen so far".

◦ Corrected sentence: This is the most moving film that I have seen so far in my career as a critic.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "This is the most moving film" is proper, with "the most" forming the superlative of the adjective "moving".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "in my career as a critic." is proper, with "in" used before "my career" and "a" used before the consonant sound of "critic".

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "saw" in part (b) is a simple past, while "so far" after a superlative needs the present perfect.

 

NOTE

 

• This is the best book I have ever read, It is the tallest building we have seen so far (superlative + present perfect with "ever" or "so far").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The inspector demanded (a)/ that the licence (b)/ of the shop (c)/ is shown immediately. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After verbs of demand, request, suggest, recommend, insist and propose followed by "that", the base form (subjunctive) of the verb is used, and "should" is optional. So "is shown" must be "be shown".

◦ Corrected sentence: The inspector demanded that the licence of the shop be shown immediately.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The inspector demanded" is proper, with the simple past "demanded" as the reporting verb.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "that the licence" is proper, with "that" introducing the noun clause.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "of the shop" is proper, with "of" showing what the licence belongs to.

 

NOTE

 

• The teacher insisted that he attend the class, The doctor suggested that she rest (base form after demand / insist / suggest), and not attends, rests.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Sunita told me that she will (a)/ visit her grandparents (b)/ the next day (c)/ and stay for a week. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In indirect speech, when the reporting verb ("told") is in the past tense, "will" changes to "would", and "the next day" also marks reported speech. So "she will" must be "she would".

◦ Corrected sentence: Sunita told me that she would visit her grandparents the next day and stay for a week.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "visit her grandparents" is proper, with the base verb after the modal and "her" agreeing with "she".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "the next day" is proper, as the reported form of "tomorrow".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "and stay for a week." is proper, with "stay" as a parallel base verb and "for" used before a period of time.

 

NOTE

 

• She said, "I will come tomorrow" → She said that she would come the next day (will changes to would after a past reporting verb).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

I would rather (a)/ you do not (b)/ discuss this matter (c)/ with anyone. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After "would rather + subject", the simple past is used to express a preference about the present or the future. So "you do not" must be "you did not".

◦ Corrected sentence: I would rather you did not discuss this matter with anyone.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "I would rather" is proper, with "would rather" expressing a preference.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "discuss this matter" is proper, because "discuss" is a transitive verb and takes no preposition.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "with anyone." is proper, with "anyone" used in a negative sense after "did not".

 

NOTE

 

• I would rather you stayed, She would rather he left early (would rather + subject + past); I would rather stay (same subject, base verb).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Take an umbrella (a)/ in case it (b)/ will rain (c)/ this evening. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "In case" (= as a precaution against) is followed by the simple present for a future possibility, and "will" is not used. So "will rain" must be "rains".

◦ Corrected sentence: Take an umbrella in case it rains this evening.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Take an umbrella" is proper, as an imperative with "an" used before the vowel sound of "umbrella".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "in case it" is proper, with "in case" introducing the clause.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "this evening." is proper, because "this evening" takes no preposition.

 

NOTE

 

• Take a jacket in case it gets cold, Keep some cash in case you need it (simple present after "in case"), and not in case it will get cold.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

I do not know (a)/ when the manager (b)/ will arrive. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is grammatically correct. "Will" is avoided in an adverb time clause ("I will call you when he comes"), but in a noun clause after "know / ask / wonder" the word "when" is a question word, so "will" is correct.

◦ Sentence as given: I do not know when the manager will arrive.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "I do not know" is proper, with "do not" followed by the base verb "know".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "when the manager" is proper, with "when" introducing an indirect question in normal (not inverted) word order.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "will arrive." is proper, with "will" used in a noun clause about a future event.

 

NOTE

 

• I don't know when he will come (noun clause, "will" allowed); I will call you when he comes (time clause, simple present).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Rina is having (a)/ two cars and (b)/ a farmhouse (c)/ in the suburbs. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Have" in the sense of possession is a stative verb and is not used in the continuous tense. So "is having" must be "has".

◦ Corrected sentence: Rina has two cars and a farmhouse in the suburbs.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "two cars and" is proper, with a plural noun after "two" and "and" joining the two possessions.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "a farmhouse" is proper, with "a" used before the consonant sound of "farmhouse".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "in the suburbs." is proper, with "in" and "the" used for a specific area.

 

NOTE

 

• She has a car, We have two dogs (possession, simple present); but She is having lunch, He is having a bath ("have" as an action, continuous allowed).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Please speak louder; I am not hearing you clearly over the phone.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. cannot hear.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Verbs of perception (hear, see, smell, taste, feel) are not used in the continuous tense. To show the ability to perceive at the moment, "can / cannot" is used with them. So "am not hearing" must be "cannot hear".

◦ Corrected sentence: Please speak louder; I cannot hear you clearly over the phone.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "have not heard" — this is a present perfect, and it does not express the present inability to hear that the request "Please speak louder" shows.

 

• Option 3: "was not hearing" — this is a past continuous, and it refers to an earlier time, while the sentence is about the present call.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because the perception verb "hear" is not used in the continuous form.

 

NOTE

 

• I can see a light, I can smell smoke, I cannot hear you (can + perception verb), and not I am seeing, I am smelling.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

If only the driver ___ the warning signal earlier, the accident could have been avoided.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. had heeded.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After "if only" (like "wish"), the past perfect expresses regret about the past. The main clause "could have been avoided" also refers to the past, so the correct verb is "had heeded".

◦ Complete sentence: If only the driver had heeded the warning signal earlier, the accident could have been avoided.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "heeded" — this is a simple past, which is used after "if only" for an unreal present, and it does not suit the past regret shown by "could have been avoided".

 

• Option 2: "would heed" — "if only" with "would" refers to a wish about the future or a complaint about a habit, and it does not suit a past event.

 

• Option 4: "has heeded" — this is a present perfect, and it is not used after "if only" for an unreal past situation.

 

NOTE

 

• If only I had studied (regret about the past); If only I knew (unreal present); If only it would stop raining (wish about the future).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Dr. Iyer has lived in this town all his life and knows every lane of it.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No improvement required.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is grammatically correct. A period that began in the past and continues up to now ("all his life") takes the present perfect, and the present verb "knows" confirms that Dr. Iyer still lives there.

◦ Sentence as given: Dr. Iyer has lived in this town all his life and knows every lane of it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "lived" — this is a simple past, which shows a finished period, and it does not suit the present verb "knows".

 

• Option 2: "had lived" — this is a past perfect, and it needs a past reference point, while the sentence is about the present.

 

• Option 3: "is living" — this is a present continuous, which shows a temporary situation, and it is not used with "all his life".

 

NOTE

 

• She has worked here all her life, I have known him since childhood (present perfect for a period that continues up to now).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

If I ___ the Finance Minister, I would reduce the tax on small businesses.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. were.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In a second conditional ("If + past, would + base verb"), the "if" clause takes the past subjunctive, and "were" is used for all persons for an unreal present situation. So the correct answer is "were".

◦ Complete sentence: If I were the Finance Minister, I would reduce the tax on small businesses.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "am" — this is an indicative present, which shows a real situation, and the sentence imagines an unreal one.

 

• Option 2: "will be" — "will" is not used in the "if" clause of a conditional sentence.

 

• Option 4: "would be" — "would" belongs to the main clause, and it is not used in the "if" clause.

 

NOTE

 

• If I were you, I would apologise, If she were here, she would help ("were" for all persons in an unreal present).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

I am going to call you yesterday, but the network was down for hours.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. was going to call.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Was / were going to + base verb" expresses an intention in the past that was not carried out. "Yesterday" and "was down" show that the sentence is in the past, so "am going to call" must be "was going to call".

◦ Corrected sentence: I was going to call you yesterday, but the network was down for hours.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "will be going to call" — this is not a standard form, and it refers to the future, while "yesterday" is in the past.

 

• Option 3: "have been going to call" — this is a present perfect continuous form, and it cannot be used with "yesterday".

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because the present "am going to" does not suit "yesterday" and the past "was down".

 

NOTE

 

• I was going to phone you, but I forgot, She was going to leave, but it rained (was / were going to for an unfulfilled past intention).

question: Select the sentence that is grammatically correct.
option_1: I have seen the manager yesterday, and he promised a reply.
option_2: The soup is tasting too salty for me.
option_3: The thief had disappeared before the police reached the spot.
option_4: The old man has died before the ambulance reached the hospital.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The thief had disappeared before the police reached the spot.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Only Option 3 is correct. Of two past actions, the earlier one takes the past perfect ("had disappeared") and the later one takes the simple past ("reached"), and "before" joins them.

◦ Correct sentence: The thief had disappeared before the police reached the spot.

 

• Each of the other three options contains a different error, explained below.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "I have seen the manager yesterday, and he promised a reply." — "yesterday" is a definite past time, so the simple past is needed: "I saw the manager yesterday".

 

• Option 2: "The soup is tasting too salty for me." — "taste" as a linking verb that describes quality is stative and is not used in the continuous: "The soup tastes too salty".

 

• Option 4: "The old man has died before the ambulance reached the hospital." — the death happened before "reached", so the earlier action needs the past perfect: "had died".

 

NOTE

 

• The thief had disappeared before the police reached (earlier action, past perfect); I saw him yesterday (definite past time, simple past); The soup tastes salty (stative use).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

No sooner had the curtain risen ___ the audience burst into applause.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. than.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "No sooner" is followed by "than", while "hardly" and "scarcely" are followed by "when" or "before". The pattern is "No sooner + had + subject + past participle + than + simple past", so the correct answer is "than".

◦ Complete sentence: No sooner had the curtain risen than the audience burst into applause.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "when" — "when" is used after "hardly" and "scarcely", and not after "no sooner".

 

• Option 2: "then" — "then" is an adverb of time and cannot join the two clauses after "no sooner".

 

• Option 3: "that" — "that" is not used as the linking word after "no sooner".

 

NOTE

 

• No sooner had he left than it began to rain; Hardly had he left when it began to rain ("no sooner … than", "hardly / scarcely … when").

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The pavements are wet, so it must rain heavily during the night.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. must have rained.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Must + have + past participle" expresses a logical conclusion about a past event. The wet pavements are the evidence, and "during the night" is past, so "must rain" must be "must have rained".

◦ Corrected sentence: The pavements are wet, so it must have rained heavily during the night.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "must be raining" — this is a deduction about an action in progress now, and it does not suit "during the night".

 

• Option 2: "must had rained" — after a modal, "have" is used and not "had".

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "must rain" does not express a conclusion about a past event.

 

NOTE

 

• He must have missed the train, She must have forgotten (must + have + V3 for a past deduction); He must be at home (present deduction).

question: Select the sentence in which the tense is used incorrectly.
option_1: The train will have left by the time we reach the station.
option_2: Had I known the truth, I would have acted differently.
option_3: Whenever it rains, the road near our house gets flooded.
option_4: The moment he saw the tiger, he has climbed the tree.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The moment he saw the tiger, he has climbed the tree.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Only Option 4 is incorrect. "The moment he saw the tiger" is a past clause, so the second action in the sequence must also be in the simple past. So "has climbed" must be "climbed".

◦ Correct sentence: The moment he saw the tiger, he climbed the tree.

 

• The other three options are correct, and each is explained below.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "The train will have left by the time we reach the station." — correct, because the future perfect "will have left" is used with "by the time" and a simple present clause.

 

• Option 2: "Had I known the truth, I would have acted differently." — correct, because this is an inverted third conditional ("Had + subject + past participle, would have + past participle").

 

• Option 3: "Whenever it rains, the road near our house gets flooded." — correct, because the simple present is used for a habitual or repeated event.

 

NOTE

 

• The moment he saw the tiger, he climbed the tree (both actions in the simple past); The moment he sees the tiger, he climbs the tree (both in the simple present).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

This time next week, we ___ on a beach in Goa, far away from all this work.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. will be relaxing.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The future continuous ("will be + verb-ing") is used for an action that will be in progress at a particular future time, and "This time next week" gives that time. So the correct answer is "will be relaxing".

◦ Complete sentence: This time next week, we will be relaxing on a beach in Goa, far away from all this work.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "would be relaxing" — "would" refers to a hypothetical or a future seen from the past, and it does not suit a direct future plan.

 

• Option 3: "will have relaxed" — this is a future perfect, which shows an action completed before a future time, while the action here is in progress at that time.

 

• Option 4: "have been relaxing" — this is a present perfect continuous, which looks back from the present and does not suit a future time.

 

NOTE

 

• This time tomorrow, I will be flying to Delhi, At 9 p.m. tonight, she will be watching the match (future continuous for an action in progress at a future moment).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

When Tarun was young, he can run five kilometres without stopping.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. could.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Can" is a present-tense modal, and "could" is its past form, used for a general ability in the past. The clause "When Tarun was young" is in the past, so "can" must be "could".

◦ Corrected sentence: When Tarun was young, he could run five kilometres without stopping.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "will be able to" — this is a future form, and it does not suit the past clause "was young".

 

• Option 2: "has been able to" — this is a present perfect, and it cannot go with the finished past period "when Tarun was young".

 

• Option 3: "is able to" — this is a present form, and it does not suit the past clause "was young".

 

NOTE

 

• When I was a child, I could swim, She could sing well in her youth (could for a past ability).

question: Select the sentence that is grammatically correct.
option_1: She asked me whether I had ever visited Assam.
option_2: I will wait at the gate until you will return from the bank.
option_3: While they were playing chess, the lights have gone out.
option_4: Ever since he was a child, he is afraid of dogs.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. She asked me whether I had ever visited Assam.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Only Option 1 is correct. In a reported question after a past reporting verb ("asked"), the present perfect of the original ("Have you ever visited Assam?") changes to the past perfect, and "whether / if" is used with normal word order.

◦ Correct sentence: She asked me whether I had ever visited Assam.

 

• Each of the other three options contains a different error, explained below.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "I will wait at the gate until you will return from the bank." — "until" introduces a time clause, where "will" is not used and the simple present is needed: "until you return".

 

• Option 3: "While they were playing chess, the lights have gone out." — a short action that interrupts a past continuous action takes the simple past: "went out".

 

• Option 4: "Ever since he was a child, he is afraid of dogs." — with "ever since" and a simple past clause, the main clause takes the present perfect: "has been afraid".

 

NOTE

 

• She asked me whether I had visited Assam (reported question); "Have you visited Assam?" → She asked if I had visited Assam (present perfect changes to past perfect).
